--- title: "How many components to keep" description: "Three ways to choose how many principal components to keep: a share of the variance, a baseline from shuffled data, and cross-validation of the model that uses the components. Then UMAP, briefly, a map made for looking at the stations." order: 5 categories: [unsupervised, data-preparation] --- ## Components can replace columns as model inputs [Principal component analysis](principal-component-analysis.qmd) kept two components because a map has two axes. Components are also used as inputs: a model can take a few components in place of 24 taxon columns that rise and fall together, and a hundred sensor channels can shrink to a handful. Then the number to keep matters. Too few leaves structure behind; too many carries noise into the next model. This page compares three ways to choose that number on the community matrix, and ends with **UMAP**, a method that makes a map of the stations for looking at rather than for modelling. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea The simplest rule keeps components until together they hold a set share of the variance, often 80%. It treats all variance as worth keeping. In counts of species much of the variance is chance, spread thinly over every column, and the rule keeps components to carry that too. Two ways do better, one for each reason to keep a component. ::: {.diagram} ![Two ways to choose the number of components. Compare each component's share of the variance with the share it reaches when every column is shuffled, and keep those above it; or, when the components feed a model, cross-validate the model at each number and keep the fewest that do as well as the best.](img/components-to-keep.svg){fig-alt="Two cards side by side, joined by the word or, with a strip of definitions below. 1 Beat the shuffled baseline: a bar chart of the share of the variance held by components 1 to 10, falling from left to right, with an orange line for the shuffled data; the first three bars rise above the line, are coloured blue and labelled kept; the rest, below it, are grey. 2 Ask the model that uses them: cross-validated error against the number of components kept falls steeply from the first point to the second and then stays flat; a dotted line one standard error above the lowest error passes just above the second point, which is marked as the fewest that do as well. The strip reads: 80% rule, keep components until they hold 80% of the variance, noise included; baseline, each column shuffled on its own, the shares components reach with no structure; cross-validation, PCA refitted in every fold, so the held-out stations stay unseen."} ::: - **A shuffled baseline** asks which components hold structure. It is the baseline of [Choosing the number of clusters](choosing-the-number-of-clusters.qmd): shuffle each column on its own, so every taxon keeps its counts but no taxa occur together. PCA of a shuffled table still gives components of unequal size, because some columns line up a little by chance and PCA finds whatever lines up. A component of the real table counts as structure when its share beats the share the same component reaches in the shuffled tables. This is called **parallel analysis**. - **Cross-validation** asks how many components a model needs. When the components feed a model, their number is a setting to tune like any other, chosen as in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). ## Worked example ### Parallel analysis keeps far fewer components than the 80% rule The community matrix gets the log, common scale and PCA of [Principal component analysis](principal-component-analysis.qmd), wrapped in a function so that shuffled copies can go through exactly the same steps. The first table gives the first component at which the cumulative share reaches 80%. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax")) percent_variance <- function(data) { recipe(~ ., data = data) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_pca(all_numeric_predictors()) |> prep() |> tidy(number = 3, type = "variance") |> filter(terms == "percent variance") |> pull(value) } shares <- tibble(component = 1:24, observed = percent_variance(taxa_only), cumulative = cumsum(observed)) shares |> filter(cumulative >= 80) |> slice_head(n = 1) |> mutate(across(-component, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| component| observed| cumulative| |---------:|--------:|----------:| | 16| 2.72| 82.68|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() community = load_coastal_community() taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax") def prepare(): return [("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler())] def percent_variance(data): pipeline = Pipeline(prepare() + [("pca", PCA())]).fit(data) return 100 * pipeline["pca"].explained_variance_ratio_ shares = pd.DataFrame({"component": np.arange(1, 25), "observed": percent_variance(taxa_only)}) shares["cumulative"] = shares["observed"].cumsum() shares[shares["cumulative"] >= 80].head(1).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | component | observed | cumulative | |------------:|-----------:|-------------:| | 16 | 2.72 | 82.68 | ::: ::: ::: The 80% rule keeps 16 of the 24 components: the first 15 hold 79.96%, just short. Keeping 16 columns in place of 24 reduces little. For the baseline, the table is shuffled 100 times and each shuffled copy goes through the same steps. A component counts when its observed share is higher than in 95 of the 100 shuffled tables, and counting stops at the first component that falls short. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shuffle_columns <- function(data) { data |> mutate(across(everything(), \(x) sample(x))) } set.seed(21) shuffled <- map(1:100, \(i) percent_variance(shuffle_columns(taxa_only))) # for each component, the share beaten by 95 of the 100 shuffled tables shares <- shares |> mutate(shuffled = map_dbl(component, \(j) quantile(map_dbl(shuffled, j), 0.95)), above = observed > shuffled) shares |> dplyr::select(component, observed, shuffled, above) |> slice_head(n = 6) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| component| observed| shuffled|above | |---------:|--------:|--------:|:-----| | 1| 15.85| 5.73|TRUE | | 2| 13.50| 5.44|TRUE | | 3| 6.17| 5.27|TRUE | | 4| 4.92| 5.13|FALSE | | 5| 4.50| 4.97|FALSE | | 6| 4.38| 4.87|FALSE |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(21) def shuffle_columns(data): return data.apply(lambda column: rng.permutation(column.to_numpy())) shuffled = np.array([percent_variance(shuffle_columns(taxa_only)) for _ in range(100)]) # for each component, the share beaten by 95 of the 100 shuffled tables shares["shuffled"] = np.quantile(shuffled, 0.95, axis=0) shares["above"] = shares["observed"] > shares["shuffled"] shares[["component", "observed", "shuffled", "above"]].head(6).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | component | observed | shuffled | above | |------------:|-----------:|-----------:|:--------| | 1 | 15.85 | 5.74 | True | | 2 | 13.5 | 5.44 | True | | 3 | 6.17 | 5.24 | True | | 4 | 4.92 | 5.12 | False | | 5 | 4.5 | 5 | False | | 6 | 4.38 | 4.88 | False | ::: ::: ::: Three components beat the baseline. PC1 and PC2 hold more than twice the share of their shuffled counterparts. PC3 holds 6.2%, against 5.3% in the shuffled tables: a smaller margin, but a clear one. PC4 falls short, at 4.9% against 5.1%. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(shares, aes(component, observed)) + geom_vline(xintercept = n_80, linetype = "dotted", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + annotate("text", x = n_80 + 0.3, y = max(shares$observed), hjust = 0, label = "80% of the variance", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) + geom_line(aes(y = shuffled), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.8) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.5) + geom_point(aes(colour = component <= n_kept), size = 2.4, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ml_palette[["blue"]], `FALSE` = ml_palette[["grey"]])) + labs(x = "component", y = "share of the variance (%)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The share of the variance held by each component of the community matrix, against the share the same component reaches in shuffled copies of it (higher than in 95 of 100 shuffles). Components above the dashed line hold structure. The dotted line marks where the 80% rule stops.](dimensionality-reduction_files/figure-html/fig-baseline-1.png){#fig-baseline fig-alt='Points joined by a line show the share of the variance against component number, from 1 to 24. The observed shares start high, at 15.9 and 13.5 per cent for the first two components, drop to 6.2 at the third and then fall slowly to 1.8 at the 24th. A dashed line for the shuffled tables falls gently from 5.7 to 3.1 per cent. The first 3 points, coloured blue, lie above the dashed line; the rest, in grey, lie on or below it. A dotted vertical line at component 16 is labelled 80% of the variance.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The figure shows why the two rules disagree. After PC3 every component holds about what the shuffled tables give it, so from there on each added component carries chance more than structure, and the 80% rule goes on adding them until it reaches component 16. ### Cross-validation keeps two components for predicting depth Taxa present at a station tell you about its habitat, so community composition is often used as an indicator. Here the components predict station depth with [linear regression](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd), and cross-validation chooses how many to use. `num_comp = tune()` marks the number of components as the setting to tune. The folds hold out whole sites, as in [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd), because stations at the same site are more alike than stations from different sites. `step_pca()` sits inside the recipe, so the PCA is fitted again on each fold's training stations and only applied to its held-out ones. Fitting it once on all 800 stations would let the held-out stations shape the components, the leakage of [Avoiding information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} depth_data <- community |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, site_id, depth_m), by = "station_id") |> dplyr::select(-station_id) depth_recipe <- recipe(depth_m ~ ., data = depth_data) |> update_role(site_id, new_role = "id") |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = tune()) set.seed(61) folds <- group_vfold_cv(depth_data, group = site_id, v = 10) tuned <- tune_grid(workflow(depth_recipe, linear_reg()), resamples = folds, grid = tibble(num_comp = c(1:8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24)), metrics = metric_set(rmse)) best <- select_best(tuned, metric = "rmse") fewest <- select_by_one_std_err(tuned, num_comp, metric = "rmse") bind_rows(`lowest error` = best, `one-standard-error rule` = fewest, .id = "choice") |> dplyr::select(choice, num_comp) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|choice | num_comp| |:-----------------------|--------:| |lowest error | 8| |one-standard-error rule | 2|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, GroupKFold depth_data = community.merge(survey[["station_id", "site_id", "depth_m"]], on="station_id") grid = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24] depth_pipeline = Pipeline(prepare() + [("pca", PCA()), ("model", LinearRegression())]) folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61) tuned = GridSearchCV(depth_pipeline, {"pca__n_components": grid}, cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") tuned = tuned.fit(depth_data.filter(like="tax"), depth_data["depth_m"], groups=depth_data["site_id"]) # One row per number of components, one column per fold, as tidymodels has it. fold_errors = -np.column_stack([tuned.cv_results_[f"split{k}_test_score"] for k in range(10)]) metrics = pd.DataFrame({"num_comp": grid, "mean": fold_errors.mean(axis=1), "std_err": fold_errors.std(axis=1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(10)}) best = metrics.loc[metrics["mean"].idxmin()] cut_off = best["mean"] + best["std_err"] fewest = metrics.loc[metrics["mean"] <= cut_off, "num_comp"].min() pd.DataFrame({"choice": ["lowest error", "one-standard-error rule"], "num_comp": [int(best["num_comp"]), int(fewest)]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | choice | num_comp | |:------------------------|-----------:| | lowest error | 4 | | one-standard-error rule | 2 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cv |> mutate(chosen = num_comp == fewest$num_comp) |> ggplot(aes(num_comp, mean)) + geom_hline(yintercept = cut_off, linetype = "dotted", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - std_err, ymax = mean + std_err), width = 0.4, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(aes(colour = chosen), size = 2.4, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], `FALSE` = ml_palette[["blue"]])) + labs(x = "number of components kept", y = "cross-validated RMSE (m)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cross-validated error when station depth is predicted from principal components of the community, folds held out by site. The bars reach one standard error either side. The dotted line is one standard error above the lowest error; the orange point is the fewest components under it.](dimensionality-reduction_files/figure-html/fig-components-1.png){#fig-components fig-alt='Points joined by a line show cross-validated RMSE in metres against the number of components kept, from 1 to 24, each with a vertical error bar. The error falls from 30.5 metres at one component to 21.2 at two, marked in orange, and stays between 20.7 and 21.2 from there to 24 components. A dotted horizontal line at 21.7 metres, one standard error above the lowest error, lies above every point from two components on.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: One component predicts depth to within 30.5 m (RMSE); two bring that to 21.2 m. After that the error hardly moves: the lowest, 20.7 m at 8 components, is within one standard error of two, so the one-standard-error rule keeps two. The baseline kept three. PC3 holds structure, but structure that says nothing about depth. Its average score on each kind of seabed shows what it holds. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} three <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = 3) |> prep() by_seabed <- community |> bind_cols(bake(three, new_data = NULL)) |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, substrate), by = "station_id") |> summarise(stations = n(), mean_PC3 = mean(PC3), .by = substrate) |> arrange(mean_PC3) by_seabed |> mutate(mean_PC3 = round(mean_PC3, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|substrate | stations| mean_PC3| |:---------|--------:|--------:| |rock | 55| -0.78| |sand | 303| -0.08| |mud | 303| 0.01| |gravel | 139| 0.47|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} scores = Pipeline(prepare() + [("pca", PCA(n_components=3))]).fit_transform(taxa_only) by_seabed = (community.assign(PC3=scores[:, 2]) .merge(survey[["station_id", "substrate"]], on="station_id") .groupby("substrate", observed=True) .agg(stations=("PC3", "size"), mean_PC3=("PC3", "mean")) .sort_values("mean_PC3") .reset_index()) by_seabed.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | substrate | stations | mean_PC3 | |:------------|-----------:|-----------:| | rock | 55 | -0.78 | | sand | 303 | -0.08 | | mud | 303 | 0.01 | | gravel | 139 | 0.47 | ::: ::: ::: PC3 separates rock (−0.78) from gravel (0.47), with mud and sand near zero. Both are hard bottom, and telling them apart adds nothing to the depth predictions. So the two methods answer different questions, and both answers are right: three components hold structure, and two are enough to predict depth. A model of something that differs between rock and gravel would need the third. ### UMAP keeps neighbours together PCA's axes are straight lines through the data. **UMAP** (uniform manifold approximation and projection) makes a flat map in a different way: it places the stations so that each one's nearest neighbours in the 24 columns stay close to it, and bends the space as much as that needs. `neighbors` sets how many neighbours each station keeps close. `step_umap()` from the embed package adds it to a recipe; in Python it comes from the umap-learn package, since scikit-learn has no UMAP. The shuffled table goes through the same steps as a baseline, and the tables give the correlation of depth with each axis of the two maps. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} umap_scores <- function(data) { recipe(~ ., data = data) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_umap(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = 2, neighbors = 15, seed = c(31, 31)) |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) } stations <- community |> dplyr::select(station_id) |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(seabed = if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "Hard bottom", "Soft bottom")) set.seed(21) maps <- bind_rows( Observed = bind_cols(stations, umap_scores(taxa_only)), Shuffled = bind_cols(stations, umap_scores(shuffle_columns(taxa_only))), .id = "data") |> mutate(data = fct_inorder(data)) maps |> summarise(UMAP1 = cor(UMAP1, depth_m), UMAP2 = cor(UMAP2, depth_m), .by = data) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|data | UMAP1| UMAP2| |:--------|-----:|-----:| |Observed | 0.27| -0.85| |Shuffled | 0.00| -0.02|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import umap def umap_scores(data): prepared = Pipeline(prepare()).fit_transform(data) return umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, random_state=31, n_jobs=1).fit_transform(prepared) stations = community[["station_id"]].merge( survey[["station_id", "depth_m", "substrate"]], on="station_id") rng = np.random.default_rng(21) maps = {"Observed": umap_scores(taxa_only), "Shuffled": umap_scores(shuffle_columns(taxa_only))} pd.DataFrame([{"data": name, "UMAP1": np.corrcoef(xy[:, 0], stations["depth_m"])[0, 1], "UMAP2": np.corrcoef(xy[:, 1], stations["depth_m"])[0, 1]} for name, xy in maps.items()]).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | data | UMAP1 | UMAP2 | |:---------|--------:|--------:| | Observed | -0.24 | 0.84 | | Shuffled | 0.06 | 0.03 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(maps, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, colour = depth_m, shape = seabed)) + geom_point(size = 1.6, alpha = 0.85) + facet_wrap(~ data, scales = "free") + labs(colour = "depth (m)", shape = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![UMAP maps of the community matrix and of a copy with every taxon shuffled on its own, made with the same settings. Colour is depth and shape is seabed; neither was given to UMAP.](dimensionality-reduction_files/figure-html/fig-umap-1.png){#fig-umap fig-alt='Two scatter plots of UMAP2 against UMAP1, one point per station, coloured from dark purple for shallow to yellow for deep and shaped by seabed. Left, observed: the hard-bottom stations, drawn as circles, form a group of their own, separated by a gap from a larger group of soft-bottom stations, drawn as triangles; within each group the colour runs smoothly from shallow at one end to deep at the other. Right, shuffled: one round cloud with circles and triangles mixed and colours scattered at random. Depth correlates 0.85 with one axis of the observed map and no more than 0.02 with either axis of the shuffled one.' width=1800} ::: ::: ::: On the observed map the hard-bottom stations form a group of their own, apart from the soft-bottom ones, and depth runs smoothly from one end of each group to the other: the boundary and the gradient of [Principal component analysis](principal-component-analysis.qmd), drawn more plainly. The shuffled map is a single cloud with depth scattered through it, and depth correlates no more than 0.02 with either of its axes, against 0.85 on the observed map. Read a UMAP map for its neighbourhoods only. Stations close together have similar communities, but the size of the gap between groups, the size of each group and the direction of the axes carry no meaning, and all of them change with `neighbors` and the seed, so report both. A UMAP map shows structure to people; for inputs to a model, components with loadings are easier to check and to explain. ## A component is harder to act on than a column "Mud below 100 m" is a finding someone can act on; "a score above 1.4 on PC2" is not, until its loadings are explained. When a result must be communicated, weigh that against the gain from fewer columns. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Keeping components until they hold **80% of the variance** keeps noise too: it kept 16 of 24 components of the community matrix. - A **shuffled baseline** (parallel analysis) keeps the components that hold more of the variance than they would in a table with each column shuffled. It kept 3. - When the components feed a model, **cross-validate** the number of components, with `step_pca()` inside the recipe so the PCA is refitted in every fold. Predicting depth needed 2. - The methods answer different questions. PC3 held structure, rock against gravel, that depth did not need. - **UMAP** keeps each station's neighbours close and bends everything else. Read only its neighbourhoods, not distances between groups or their sizes, and run a shuffled copy through the same steps. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Make the UMAP maps again with `neighbors = 5` and with `neighbors = 50`. Which features of the observed map stay, and does the shuffled map change? 2. Replace `linear_reg()` with `rand_forest(mode = "regression")` in the tuning workflow. Does a more flexible model make use of more components?
